cases.rationale: nta2025:s187 (c) zero-rates educational books (nta2025:s189:def:educational-books); nta2025:s156 (4) says a 0%-rated supplier pays VAT on inputs and may request a refund.
cases.question: We sell school textbooks. Do we charge VAT on them, and can we get back the VAT we pay our printers?

claims.text: VAT is paid on all taxable supplies in Nigeria, subject to the exemptions in Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act.
Educational books and materials are among the taxable supplies charged to VAT at the rate of 0%. This is subject to paragraph 2 of the Thirtenth Schedule to the Act.

"Educational books" means physical or electronic books used to implement instruction and facilitate learning in educational institutions providing pre-primary, primary, secondary, tertiary, special, adult, vocational, technical science or religious education. The definition includes booklets, brochures, pamphlets and leaflets, newspapers, journals and periodicals, children's books, picture and painting books, music, maps, charts and topographical plans, and covers, cases and other articles supplied together with the books.
A taxable person pays VAT to a supplier on the taxable supply made to the person. The VAT paid is known as input VAT.
A person whose supplies are chargeable to VAT at 0% shall pay VAT on taxable supplies consumed in the production of its supplies, and may thereafter request a refund of the VAT paid.
A taxable person is entitled to a refund of excess VAT not utilised as a credit, upon request to the Service and provision of such information or documents as the Service may require.

Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, a taxable person is entitled to use the excess as a credit against subsequent months. This applies not later than the due date for rendering the relevant tax return prescribed by the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025.

Input tax on a taxable supply may be deducted, but only to the extent it was incurred for consumption, use or supply in the course of making taxable supplies. Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to taxable supplies may be deducted. The input tax is allowable for deduction within five years after the end of the tax period in which it was incurred.
The input tax that may be deducted is limited to taxable supplies made as from the commencement of this Act.

cases.rendered:
VAT is paid on all taxable supplies in Nigeria, subject to the exemptions in Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 145]

Educational books and materials are among the taxable supplies charged to VAT at the rate of 0%. This is subject to paragraph 2 of the Thirtenth Schedule to the Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 187]

"Educational books" means physical or electronic books used to implement instruction and facilitate learning in educational institutions providing pre-primary, primary, secondary, tertiary, special, adult, vocational, technical science or religious education. The definition includes booklets, brochures, pamphlets and leaflets, newspapers, journals and periodicals, children's books, picture and painting books, music, maps, charts and topographical plans, and covers, cases and other articles supplied together with the books. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 189, definition of "educational books"]

A taxable person pays VAT to a supplier on the taxable supply made to the person. The VAT paid is known as input VAT. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 152]

A person whose supplies are chargeable to VAT at 0% shall pay VAT on taxable supplies consumed in the production of its supplies, and may thereafter request a refund of the VAT paid. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

A taxable person is entitled to a refund of excess VAT not utilised as a credit, upon request to the Service and provision of such information or documents as the Service may require. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

Where input VAT exceeds output VAT, a taxable person is entitled to use the excess as a credit against subsequent months. This applies not later than the due date for rendering the relevant tax return prescribed by the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

Input tax on a taxable supply may be deducted, but only to the extent it was incurred for consumption, use or supply in the course of making taxable supplies. Where input tax is incurred in making both taxable and non-taxable supplies, only the proportion relating to taxable supplies may be deducted. The input tax is allowable for deduction within five years after the end of the tax period in which it was incurred. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

The input tax that may be deducted is limited to taxable supplies made as from the commencement of this Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

- Paragraph 2 of the Thirtenth Schedule, to which section 187 is subject, is not among the passages.
- The passages do not say whether the business's textbooks fall within the definition of educational books, or whether the printers' services are taxable supplies.
- The passages do not say whether the business is a taxable person or a registered person.

- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 187 (gazette pages A 490, A 491)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 189, definition of "educational books" (gazette page A 492)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 152 (gazette page A 473)

claims.text: Where a Nigerian company declares dividend out of profits on which no tax is payable because there are no total profits, or because total profits are less than the dividend declared, the company paying the dividend is charged to tax. This rule does not apply to franked investment income as provided in the Act.

claims.text: A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies.

Where a non-resident person is making taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria shall withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service.
The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier of taxable supplies, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service.

Where a person appointed under subsection (3) has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person shall not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the person appointed has failed to collect the VAT.
A non-resident person that makes a taxable supply to a person in Nigeria may appoint a representative for the purpose of compliance with its VAT obligations.

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom taxable supplies is made in Nigeria and issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service.

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under section 155 shall be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service.

The remission must be accompanied by a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates.

Federal, State and Local Government bodies and their Ministries, Departments or Agencies, and any other person appointed by the Service, shall collect or withhold VAT on taxable supplies made to them and remit it to the Service.

<question>
I pay a foreign online company with no office in Nigeria for software services. Who has to account for the VAT?
</question>
<gaps>
<gap index="0">
The passages do not say whether the Service has appointed this supplier to collect VAT, so which route applies is not known.
</gap>
</gaps>

cases.rendered:
A non-resident person who makes taxable supplies to Nigeria shall register for tax and include VAT on its invoice for all taxable supplies. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

Where a non-resident person is making taxable supplies from outside Nigeria to persons in Nigeria, the taxable person to whom the supply is made in Nigeria shall withhold the VAT due on the supply and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may, by notice, appoint any person, including a non-resident supplier of taxable supplies, to collect the VAT and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

Where a person appointed under subsection (3) has made a taxable supply to a taxable person in Nigeria, the taxable person shall not have the obligation to withhold the VAT, except where the person appointed has failed to collect the VAT. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

A non-resident person that makes a taxable supply to a person in Nigeria may appoint a representative for the purpose of compliance with its VAT obligations. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151]

The Service may direct a taxable person to whom taxable supplies is made in Nigeria and issued an invoice on which VAT is not included, to self-account for the VAT payable and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

VAT collected, withheld or self-accounted under section 155 shall be remitted to the Service on or before the 14th day of the month immediately following the month of the transaction or as may be prescribed by the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

The remission must be accompanied by a schedule showing the name, Tax ID and address of the contractor or supplier, invoice number, gross amount of invoice, amount of the VAT and the month to which the return relates. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

Federal, State and Local Government bodies and their Ministries, Departments or Agencies, and any other person appointed by the Service, shall collect or withhold VAT on taxable supplies made to them and remit it to the Service. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The passages do not say whether software services are taxable supplies.
- The passages do not say whether the foreign online company in the question is a non-resident person or whether the buyer is a taxable person.
- The passages do not say whether the Service has appointed this supplier to collect VAT, so which route applies is not known.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 151 (gazette pages A 472, A 473)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 155 (gazette page A 474)

This is a research and reference tool. It is not tax advice and is not a substitute for a licensed tax professional. It must not be used for an actual filing or compliance decision. Answers come only from the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 and selected parts of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 (Official Gazette text, corpus snapshot 18 October 2026).

claims.text: VAT is paid on all taxable supplies in Nigeria, subject to the exemptions in Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act.
VAT is charged on the value of all taxable supplies at the rate of 7.5%, subject to the provisions of Part IV of Chapter Eight of the Act.
Basic food items are taxable supplies charged to VAT at the rate of 0%, subject to paragraph 2 of the Thirtenth Schedule to the Act.

"Basic food items" means an agriculture-based or aquatic-based staple food, and the definition includes cereals such as rice, in the form of grain, flour or crop, whether raw or semi-processed, whether in bulk or retail.

The definition of basic food items includes flour and starch, including cassava flakes (garri), whether bleached or unbleached, refined or unrefined, provided that it is suitable for culinary purposes.

gaps: Paragraph 2 of the Thirtenth Schedule, to which the 0% rate is made subject, is not among the passages.
Whether the rice and garri sold in the shop are in a form and quality that fits the definitions (for example, suitable for culinary purposes) is a question of fact the passages do not settle.
Whether the shop's sales are taxable supplies by the seller, and any VAT registration or return duties, are not covered by the passages.

claims.text: Table I of the Part sets the rate of capital allowance by class of qualifying capital expenditure. Class 3 has a rate of 25% and lists Motor Vehicle Expenditure among its items.

Where a person has incurred qualifying expenditure wholly and exclusively for the purposes of its trade or business, an allowance is made for each year of assessment in the basis period for which the asset was used for that trade or business, at the rate specified in Table I.
A capital allowance for an asset is made for a year of assessment if, at the end of a basis period, the person owns the asset and used it for the purposes of its trade or business.
Where the basis period for a year of assessment is less than one year, the allowance for that year is granted proportionately.
An allowance is not made for a year unless it is claimed for that year, or the relevant tax authority is of the opinion that it would be just to the taxpayer and reasonable to do so.

The allowance is subtracted from the remainder of the assessable profits or income for the year. Any part that cannot be fully deducted for lack of remainder is treated as a deduction for the next year, and for succeeding years until fully utilised.

Where a capital allowance was granted for an asset before the commencement of the Act, the remaining basis periods are the number of years of assessment for which allowance is to be made under the Part less the number of years for which allowance was previously made.

Table I of the Part sets the rate of capital allowance by class of qualifying capital expenditure. Class 3 has a rate of 25% and lists Motor Vehicle Expenditure among its items. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, Table I, Capital Allowance]

Where a person has incurred qualifying expenditure wholly and exclusively for the purposes of its trade or business, an allowance is made for each year of assessment in the basis period for which the asset was used for that trade or business, at the rate specified in Table I. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, paragraphs 6 to 8]

A capital allowance for an asset is made for a year of assessment if, at the end of a basis period, the person owns the asset and used it for the purposes of its trade or business. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, paragraphs 6 to 8]

Where the basis period for a year of assessment is less than one year, the allowance for that year is granted proportionately. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, paragraphs 6 to 8]

An allowance is not made for a year unless it is claimed for that year, or the relevant tax authority is of the opinion that it would be just to the taxpayer and reasonable to do so. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, paragraphs 21 to 22]

The allowance is subtracted from the remainder of the assessable profits or income for the year. Any part that cannot be fully deducted for lack of remainder is treated as a deduction for the next year, and for succeeding years until fully utilised. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, First Schedule, Part I, paragraphs 21 to 22]

Where a capital allowance was granted for an asset before the commencement of the Act, the remaining basis periods are the number of years of assessment for which allowance is to be made under the Part less the number of years for which allowance was previously made. claims.text: Where the relevant tax authority discovers or is of the opinion, at any time, that a taxable person liable to tax has not been assessed or has been assessed at less than ought to have been charged, it may, within six years of the assessment, assess the taxable person at the amount or additional amount that ought to have been charged.
The six-year limit does not stop the relevant tax authority from continuing a tax audit and raising an additional assessment, where the tax audit began before the six-year limit expired.

Despite the time limit, where a taxable person makes a deliberate misstatement in connection with any tax imposed under the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 or any other tax law, the relevant tax authority may at any time, and as often as necessary, assess the taxable person to the amount or additional amount needed to make good any loss of tax attributable to the deliberate misstatement.
All relevant facts are to be considered in working out the additional tax, even where those facts were not known when an earlier assessment or additional assessment was made for the same year.
The provisions of the Act on notice of assessment, appeal and other proceedings apply to an additional assessment and to the tax charged.

Section 41 does not prevent the tax authority from making an assessment or additional assessment for a year, if it does not re-open any issue on the same facts that was determined for that year of assessment under section 41(5) by agreement or on appeal.

Where the relevant tax authority discovers or is of the opinion, at any time, that a taxable person liable to tax has not been assessed or has been assessed at less than ought to have been charged, it may, within six years of the assessment, assess the taxable person at the amount or additional amount that ought to have been charged. The six-year limit does not stop the relevant tax authority from continuing a tax audit and raising an additional assessment, where the tax audit began before the six-year limit expired. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 36]

Despite the time limit, where a taxable person makes a deliberate misstatement in connection with any tax imposed under the Nigeria Tax Act, 2025 or any other tax law, the relevant tax authority may at any time, and as often as necessary, assess the taxable person to the amount or additional amount needed to make good any loss of tax attributable to the deliberate misstatement. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 36]

All relevant facts are to be considered in working out the additional tax, even where those facts were not known when an earlier assessment or additional assessment was made for the same year. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 36]

The provisions of the Act on notice of assessment, appeal and other proceedings apply to an additional assessment and to the tax charged. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 36]

Section 41 does not prevent the tax authority from making an assessment or additional assessment for a year, if it does not re-open any issue on the same facts that was determined for that year of assessment under section 41(5) by agreement or on appeal. A taxable person is entitled to a refund of excess VAT not used as a credit, upon request to the Service and provision of such information or documents as the Service may require. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 156]

For tax refunds under the general refund section, a refund due shall be made within 90 days of the decision of the relevant tax authority made under subsection (2) of that section, with the option of a set-off against any tax liability of the taxpayer. claims.text: Section 192 is about transactions between related parties, which are to be at arm's length.
A company involved in an arrangement with a related party shall ensure that the terms and conditions of the arrangement are at arm's length.

cases.question: My company made ₦120 million profit this year. How much company income tax will it pay?

claims.text: Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company. A small company is taxed at 0%.
Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of this Act.

The total profits of a company are its total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains, less any loss ascertained in accordance with subsection (6) and capital allowance under Part I of the First Schedule.

A company includes dividend income in its profits, gross of any tax paid or deducted at source. Dividends a Nigerian company receives by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax.

Despite any other provision, if a company's effective tax rate in a year of assessment is less than 15%, it must recompute and pay additional tax to bring the rate to 15%. This applies to a constituent entity of an MNE group and to any other company with aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment.

gaps: The definition of a small company is not among the passages, so whether the company is taxed at 0% or 30 per cent cannot be determined.

Tax is levied for each year of assessment on the total profits of every company. A small company is taxed at 0%. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

Any other company is taxed at the rate of 30 per cent from the commencement of this Act. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56]

The total profits of a company are its total assessable profits from all sources, including chargeable gains, less any loss ascertained in accordance with subsection (6) and capital allowance under Part I of the First Schedule. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4)]

A company includes dividend income in its profits, gross of any tax paid or deducted at source. Dividends a Nigerian company receives by way of shares of the paying company are not included in its profits chargeable to tax. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8]

Despite any other provision, if a company's effective tax rate in a year of assessment is less than 15%, it must recompute and pay additional tax to bring the rate to 15%. This applies to a constituent entity of an MNE group and to any other company with aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 and above in the relevant year of assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- The definition of a small company is not among the passages, so whether the company is taxed at 0% or 30 per cent cannot be determined.
- The company's total profits after losses and capital allowances are not given, and the question gives only a profit figure, so the tax amount cannot be worked out.
- Applying the rate to the profit is a calculation that is not done here.
- The company's turnover and whether it belongs to an MNE group are not given, so whether the 15% effective tax rate rule applies cannot be determined.
- Subsection (6) of section 27, which that section refers to, is not among the passages.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56 (gazette page A 426)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4) (gazette pages A 412, A 413)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8 (gazette page A 397)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57 (gazette page A 426)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 56: The National Assembly text lets the President, on the advice of the National Economic Council, reduce the 30% rate to 25% by order; the gazette has no such provision. (DR-050)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 27(1) to (4): The National Assembly text requires companies in the priority sector to obtain a certificate of acceptance from the Industrial Inspectorate Department for qualifying capital expenditure; the gazette has no such condition. (DR-039)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 8: Cross-reference: the gazette cites section 51 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, the National Assembly text section 50. (DR-007, DR-008)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The minimum tax is measured differently. Gazette: covered tax paid divided by profits, where profits are net profit before tax less 5% of depreciation and personnel cost. National Assembly: covered taxes (companies income tax, petroleum profit tax, hydrocarbon tax, development levy, priority sector tax credit) as a percentage of net income, which excludes franked investment income and unrealised gains or losses. (DR-051)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette applies the 15% minimum to every constituent entity of an MNE group; the National Assembly text only where the group's turnover is at least 750 million (printed with a pound sign) or its equivalent. (DR-052)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The 15% minimum effective tax rate applies from an aggregate turnover of ₦20,000,000,000 in the gazette and ₦50,000,000,000 in the National Assembly text. (DR-053)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The National Assembly text exempts approved free-zone enterprises (except for sales into the customs territory and MNE entities) and lets the Service set a higher turnover threshold by regulation; the gazette has neither and measures turnover in the relevant year of assessment rather than the financial year. (DR-054)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 57: The gazette numbers the subsections (1), (2) and (4), with no (3); the labels are kept as printed. The National Assembly text has (1) to (4). (DR-055)

cases.question: Under section 191 of the Nigeria Tax Act, where do objections and appeals go?

claims.text: Under section 191, where a relevant tax authority thinks a transaction that reduces or may reduce tax payable is artificial or fictitious, it may disregard it or direct adjustments, and issue an assessment or additional assessment.

Under section 41 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, a taxable person who disputes an assessment may apply to the relevant tax authority for revision and amendment, by written notice of objection delivered in person, by courier service or via electronic means.

Where the taxable person and the relevant tax authority do not agree on the tax to be assessed, or the authority considers the notice of objection invalid, the taxpayer may exercise the right of appeal.
A party dissatisfied with the decision of the High Court may appeal to the Court of Appeal, and an appeal against the judgement of the Court of Appeal is to the Supreme Court.

cases.rendered:
Under section 191, where a relevant tax authority thinks a transaction that reduces or may reduce tax payable is artificial or fictitious, it may disregard it or direct adjustments, and issue an assessment or additional assessment. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 191]

The provisions on objections and appeals under Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 apply to a direction made under section 191. [Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 191]

Under section 41 of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, a taxable person who disputes an assessment may apply to the relevant tax authority for revision and amendment, by written notice of objection delivered in person, by courier service or via electronic means. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(1) to (4)]

Where the taxable person and the relevant tax authority do not agree on the tax to be assessed, or the authority considers the notice of objection invalid, the taxpayer may exercise the right of appeal. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8)]

A party dissatisfied with the decision of the High Court may appeal to the Court of Appeal, and an appeal against the judgement of the Court of Appeal is to the Supreme Court. [Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8)]

Not covered by the retrieved provisions:
- Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, which section 191 names, is not among the passages.
- The passages do not say which body or court first hears an appeal before the High Court.

Sources
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 191 (gazette page A 497)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(1) to (4) (gazette pages A 284, A 285)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8) (gazette page A 285)

Differences between official texts
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8): The Gombe print requires a taxpayer appealing from the Tax Appeal Tribunal to the High Court to pay 20% of the disputed amount first; the cited print has no deposit clause, and Gombe's (9) is its (8). (DR-229)
- Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025, section 41(5) to (8): The cited print's s41(8) provides appeals from the High Court to the Court of Appeal and then the Supreme Court; the National Assembly text has no such subsection. (DR-231)
- Nigeria Tax Act 2025, section 191: As printed, section 191(2) refers objections and appeals to Chapter Four of the Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025. In the cited NRS print of that Act, Chapter Four is Offences and Penalties; objections are in Chapter Two (section 41), which Nigeria Tax Act section 10(7) cites. (DQ-16)
